engines.name: Kahn · FIFO queue
engines.purpose: Build an order that respects every prerequisite.
engines.equation: d(v) = # unfinished predecessors; choose only d(v) = 0
engines.symbols: d(v): remaining indegree · V: tasks · E: dependencies
engines.invariant: Every task in the output had no unfinished prerequisite when selected.
engines.cost: The core queue algorithm is O(|V| + |E|) time and O(|V|) auxiliary space. Frame creation is excluded.
engines.limit: A valid order does not minimize storage or completion time. The cyclic remainder may also contain tasks downstream of a cycle.
engines.question: Does changing only the ready-task selection alter the order, the work, or both?

refs.title: Python graphlib — ready tasks and dependency ordering

engines.name: Kahn · LIFO stack
engines.purpose: See how taking the newest ready task changes a valid order.
engines.equation: u = most recently added ready task
engines.symbols: LIFO: last in, first out
engines.invariant: Only zero-indegree tasks may be popped.
engines.cost: O(|V| + |E|) core time; O(|V|) auxiliary space.
engines.limit: LIFO does not guarantee depth-first-search order or a better application result.
engines.question: Which input structures make FIFO and LIFO diverge?

refs.title: Python graphlib — ready tasks and dependency ordering
NetworkX — DAG algorithms and source code

engines.name: Kahn · fixed priorities
engines.purpose: Prefer the highest-scoring task among the eligible tasks.
engines.equation: u = arg max ready priority(v); smallest task ID breaks ties
engines.symbols: priority(v): fixed input score; not a memory estimate
engines.invariant: The heap contains only eligible tasks, ordered by fixed priority.
engines.cost: O(|E| + |V| log |V|) with a binary heap, excluding tracing.
engines.limit: Fixed priorities do not demonstrate changing file-release credits.
engines.question: Does maintaining a dynamic score cost more than selecting by a fixed one?

refs.title: Python heapq — priority updates and stale entries
NetworkX — DAG algorithms and source code

engines.name: Kahn · alphabetical tie-breaking
engines.purpose: Produce a deterministic alphabetical topological order.
engines.equation: u = smallest task ID in the ready set
engines.symbols: Task IDs are ordered as strings in this lesson.
steps: Build a min-heap of ready IDs
engines.invariant: The smallest currently eligible ID is always selected.
engines.cost: O(|E| + |V| log |V|) core time using a binary heap.
engines.limit: A deterministic order is not necessarily a good scheduling order.
engines.question: Which parts of a claimed improvement are only tie-breaking changes?

refs.title: NetworkX — DAG algorithms and source code
Python heapq — priority updates and stale entries

engines.name: Topological generations
engines.purpose: Reveal dependency layers, one completed layer at a time.
engines.equation: g(v) = 0 for sources; otherwise 1 + max predecessor g(u)
engines.symbols: g(v): generation number
engines.invariant: Every predecessor of a task appears in an earlier generation.
engines.cost: O(|V| + |E|) core work.
engines.limit: This models eligibility rounds, not actual parallel workers or the historical parallel-sorting algorithm.
engines.question: How much parallelism is available before hardware constraints are considered?

refs.title: Python graphlib — ready tasks and dependency ordering

engines.name: DFS topological ordering
engines.purpose: Follow dependencies deeply and reverse their finishing order.
engines.equation: order = reverse(finish list)
engines.symbols: Active: on recursion stack · Finished: all successors explored
engines.invariant: An edge to an active task proves a directed cycle; a DAG edge finishes its target first.
engines.cost: O(|V| + |E|) traversal; O(|V|) stack and state.
engines.limit: The recursive teaching version is limited to small graphs. Its finish list is not the output until reversed.
engines.question: Which errors are detectable by an independent DFS check of a Kahn implementation?

engines.name: BFS reachability
engines.purpose: Find an unweighted path using a queue.
engines.equation: distance(v) = distance(parent(v)) + 1
engines.symbols: Source and target come from the editable input.
engines.invariant: The first discovery of a task gives its shortest unweighted distance from the source.
engines.cost: O(|V| + |E|) worst-case traversal; O(|V|) state.
engines.limit: A BFS traversal order is not generally a topological order.
engines.question: How many edges need inspection to certify one relevant reachability fact?

refs.title: NetworkX — breadth-first traversal

engines.name: BFS with an edge budget
engines.purpose: See why stopping early must return UNKNOWN.
engines.equation: examined edges ≤ B; exhausted budget ⇒ UNKNOWN
engines.symbols: B: a limit on edge inspections, not on all runtime work.
engines.invariant: Every FOUND result has a real path; UNKNOWN makes no absence claim.
engines.cost: At most B edge inspections. Queue setup, snapshots and other work are not bounded by B.
engines.limit: A budget can miss useful certificates. This teaching rule is not a claimed new algorithm.
engines.question: What evidence would justify a search budget without silently changing correctness?

refs.title: NetworkX — breadth-first traversal

engines.name: Transitive reduction · reference
engines.purpose: Remove direct dependencies already implied by a longer path.
engines.equation: remove u → v iff v remains reachable from u without that edge
engines.symbols: Reachability is preserved; edge metadata has no role in this example.
engines.invariant: Every removed edge has an alternative path in the original DAG.
engines.cost: The clear reference performs one O(|V| + |E|) search per edge. Not an optimized implementation.
engines.limit: Requires a DAG here. Graph simplification is not automatically file-counter reduction.
engines.question: Could discovering a redundant relation cost more than maintaining the original state?

refs.title: NetworkX — transitive reduction

engines.name: Enumerate all topological orders
engines.purpose: Try every legal next choice on a small DAG.
engines.equation: orders(G) = every permutation satisfying position(u) < position(v)
engines.symbols: Prefix: choices already made in the current branch.
engines.invariant: Every saved order respects all edges; backtracking explores every eligible branch.
engines.cost: Output-sensitive and potentially factorial. Limited to 6 tasks in the viewer.
engines.limit: Generic backtracking, not a reproduction of the optimized Knuth–Szwarcfiter or Pruesse–Ruskey generation methods.
engines.question: Can exhaustive small cases serve as a correctness oracle rather than a production algorithm?

refs.title: NetworkX — DAG algorithms and source code

engines.name: Longest paths in a DAG
engines.purpose: Compute earliest finishes under unlimited processors and zero transfer delay.
engines.equation: EF(v) ← max(EF(v), EF(u) + duration(v))
engines.symbols: EF: earliest finish · duration: fixed input execution time.
engines.invariant: When a task is processed, every predecessor finish value is final.
engines.cost: O(|V| + |E|) after a topological traversal.
engines.limit: This is a dependency lower bound for more constrained systems, not a scheduler for a fixed number of processors.
engines.question: Are the experiments measuring ordering overhead or actual workflow completion?

refs.title: NetworkX — DAG algorithms and source code

engines.name: Edge insertion · recompute reference
engines.purpose: Distinguish a harmless forward edge, a backward edge and a new cycle.
engines.equation: position(u) < position(v) ⇒ retain order; v ⇝ u ⇒ reject u → v
engines.symbols: The input includes an old order and one inserted edge.
engines.invariant: The accepted order respects all old edges and the new edge.
engines.cost: O(|V| + |E|) full-recomputation branch; this viewer also validates the old order.
engines.limit: Not AHRSZ, MNR, a predictive algorithm or Pearce–Kelly.
engines.question: Which updates actually invalidate the previous order?

engines.name: Pearce–Kelly · repair rule
engines.purpose: Discover affected forward and backward sets, then reuse their positions.
engines.equation: affected positions ← B in old order, followed by F in old order
engines.symbols: F: reached from new target inside interval · B: reaches new source inside interval.
engines.invariant: Relative order inside F and inside B is preserved; all other task slots remain fixed.
engines.cost: The independent viewer scans the old array to collect sets and positions. It does not reproduce the paper’s exact operation counts.
engines.limit: Single insertion only. No batch optimization, predictions, or temporary-cycle tolerance.

engines.name: Tarjan strongly connected components
engines.purpose: Find mutually reachable groups and distinguish cycles from a DAG.
engines.equation: low(u) = smallest active index reachable under the DFS low-link rules
engines.symbols: Index: discovery order · Low link: earliest reachable active index.
engines.invariant: A root with low(u) = index(u) closes exactly one active strongly connected component.
engines.cost: O(|V| + |E|) traversal; O(|V|) state.
engines.limit: Static Tarjan teaching version. Not incremental strong-component maintenance with predictions.

engines.name: Priority updates and stale entries
engines.purpose: Change a priority without letting an obsolete entry win.
engines.equation: valid entry ⇔ stored version = current task version
engines.symbols: Higher score wins; task ID breaks ties.
engines.invariant: Every returned entry is current, even if stale entries remain in the heap.
engines.cost: O(log H) per heap operation; H includes stale entries. Trace tables are extra work.
engines.limit: Stale entries consume memory and must eventually be popped or rebuilt.

engines.symbols: s(v): ready-task priority · C(f): original consumer set · r*: priority counter, saturated at one.
engines.invariant: With the stated model, reduced metadata preserves scores of ready tasks and the same task order. Scores of blocked tasks need not match.
engines.cost: Exact operation counts are shown for the small input. Snapshot costs are not algorithm timings.

engines.name: HEFT · two processors
engines.purpose: Rank tasks, inspect processor gaps and minimize each chosen task’s earliest finish.
engines.equation: rank(u) = avg cost(u) + maxᵥ[comm + rank(v)]; choose min EFT(u,p)
engines.symbols: EFT: earliest finish time · comm: uniform transfer cost between different processors.
engines.invariant: Every assigned task starts after all predecessor transfers and fits a free processor interval.
engines.cost: This two-processor implementation scans sorted intervals for insertion. Trace generation is not a timing benchmark.
engines.limit: No processor-memory limits, migration, replication, failures, or adaptive estimation. The heuristic is not globally optimal.

steps: Sort affected task IDs by position

S0.name: Lasser
S0.note: Shows Kahn source removal, not Lasser’s historical procedure.

sources.title: Lasser (1961), Topological ordering of a list of randomly-numbered elements of a network
Kahn (1962), Topological sorting of large networks

S0.mechanism: An early published treatment of topological ordering of numbered network elements.
S0.limit: Only its bibliographic role is used here; no unverified complexity or priority claim.

S1.name: Kahn’s algorithm

sources.title: Topological Sorting of Large Networks

S1.mechanism: Select tasks with no unfinished prerequisites, then update their successors.
S1.limit: A valid order is not necessarily the best order for storage or runtime.

S2.name: FIFO and LIFO
S2.note: Switch between FIFO and LIFO on the same input.

sources.title: Python, graphlib documentation
Dask, Scheduling Policy documentation

S2.mechanism: Select the oldest or newest eligible vertex.
S2.limit: Different orders can result; neither optimizes every secondary objective.

S3.name: Priority Kahn
S3.note: Fixed-priority and alphabetical variants are both available.

sources.title: NetworkX, lexicographical_topological_sort documentation
Python, heapq, Priority Queue Implementation Notes

S3.mechanism: Choose an eligible vertex by a deterministic key, commonly with a heap.
S3.limit: Heap operations cost more than a FIFO queue; the quality depends on the key.

S4.name: Topological generations

sources.title: NetworkX, topological_generations documentation
Python, graphlib documentation

S4.mechanism: Produce layers whose predecessors occur in earlier layers.
S4.limit: Eligibility does not imply enough processors or memory; layer barriers can be restrictive.

S5.name: DFS ordering
S5.note: Reverse DFS finish order with cycle detection.

sources.title: Sedgewick and Wayne, Algorithms, Directed Graphs companion material

S5.mechanism: Reverse DFS completion order on a DAG.
S5.limit: Does not directly expose the same dynamic ready-set priority policy.

S6.name: Order enumeration
S6.note: Generic backtracking, not the optimized original enumeration program.

sources.title: Knuth and Szwarcfiter (1974), A structured program to generate all topological sorting arrangements

S6.mechanism: Knuth and Szwarcfiter generate multiple valid topological arrangements.
S6.limit: The number of orders can be enormous.

S7.note: Does not implement the Pruesse–Ruskey generation algorithm.

sources.title: Pruesse and Ruskey (1994), Generating Linear Extensions Fast

S7.limit: Explicitly writing every complete order still has an output cost; total enumeration can remain infeasible.

D1.note: Shows the edge-insertion problem, not AHRSZ discovery or order labels.

D10.note: No Katriel–Bodlaender order-maintenance mechanism is implemented.

D4.note: Independent single-edge core; array collection costs differ from the paper.

M1.note: Not Liu’s tree-pebbling optimum or exact buffer model.

M4.note: No optimal-peak-preserving graph transformation is claimed.

sources.title: Graph Transformations for Memory Peak Minimization by Scheduling

M4.mechanism: Apply four optimality-preserving transformations, then search the remaining graph.
M4.limit: Residual search and dataflow expansion can remain expensive.

M5.name: HEFT
M5.note: Independent two-processor HEFT with insertion and uniform communication.

sources.title: Topcuoglu, Hariri and Wu (2002), Performance-effective and low-complexity task scheduling for heterogeneous computing

M5.mechanism: Rank tasks and assign them to heterogeneous processors.
M5.limit: Requires processor and cost assumptions; does not optimize just order-construction overhead.

M6.name: Memory-aware HEFT

sources.title: Memory-aware Adaptive Scheduling of Scientific Workflows on Heterogeneous Architectures

M6.mechanism: Adapt HEFT to memory constraints and runtime information.
M6.limit: Some variants are costly to construct; changing the eviction order gave comparable results.

M7.name: Dask ordering
M7.note: Generic fixed-priority Kahn, not Dask’s production ordering policy.

sources.title: Dask Ordering

M7.mechanism: Choose priorities from task-graph structure to influence data retention.
M7.limit: Static ordering and distributed scheduling differ; neither implies global optimality.

M8.name: Least Reference Count
M8.note: Eviction priority only, not the full LRC caching system.

sources.title: LRC: Dependency-Aware Cache Management for Data Analytics Clusters

M8.mechanism: Count unfinished dependent computations to choose which cached data to retain.
M8.limit: Some tested workloads gained little from caching; the experiment also controlled page caching.

M9.name: Pegasus cleanup
M9.note: Last-use cleanup under a simple model, not the Pegasus planner.

sources.title: Pegasus Data Management

M9.mechanism: Plan file cleanup after required uses and transfers complete.
M9.limit: Per-file planning may be costly; transfers and declared dependencies matter.

P0.name: Local score model
P0.note: The simplified score policy used by the retained proof companion.

sources.title: Kahn (1962), Topological sorting of large networks
NetworkX, lexicographical_topological_sort documentation
WfCommons, Montage execution instances and task counts

P0.mechanism: For ready v, priority equals releasable generated-file bytes minus its original output bytes.
P0.limit: The score is a heuristic, not an optimal-memory guarantee; full recomputation is a correctness oracle, not a strong runtime baseline.

P1.name: Incremental counters
P1.note: Priority counters stop at one; not deletion counters.

sources.title: Yu et al. (2017), LRC: Dependency-Aware Cache Management for Data Analytics Clusters
Python, heapq, Priority Queue Implementation Notes
Dask, Scheduling Policy documentation

P1.mechanism: Use incremental counters, initialize singleton release credits, and batch heap refreshes by affected task.
P1.limit: Still updates separate counters for files whose state may be redundant.

P2.name: Equal consumer sets
P2.note: Identical original consumer sets share one weighted counter.

sources.title: WfCommons, Montage execution instances and task counts
Mt-KaHyPar, parallel hyperedge deduplication implementation

P2.mechanism: Share a counter across files with identical consumer sets; sum release bytes but retain original producer costs.
P2.limit: Grouping has a cost; generic aggregation is old; dependency-forced final consumers can be a stronger simplification.

P3.name: Forced final consumer
P3.note: Static credit emerges when dependencies force one final consumer.

sources.title: WfCommons, Montage execution instances and task counts

P3.mechanism: When all other consumers precede one consumer, assign its release credit statically and remove the dynamic counter.
P3.limit: Checking the condition costs work; arbitrary consumer sets need not have a forced final consumer.

P4.name: Consumer reduction
P4.note: Exact reachability reduction of priority metadata, not graph dependencies.

sources.title: WfCommons, Montage execution instances and task counts
Fradet, Girault and Honorat (2025), Graph Transformations for Memory Peak Minimization by Scheduling
Yu et al. (2017), LRC: Dependency-Aware Cache Management for Data Analytics Clusters

P4.mechanism: Track only consumers with no later consumer reachable through dependencies; fold a singleton into static release credit.
P4.limit: Reachability preprocessing may cost more than the updates removed; exact prior-art search remains necessary.

P5.name: Sort or scan (example)
P5.note: Equivalent subroutine outputs; no speedup or novelty assumed.

sources.title: Pearce and Kelly, A Dynamic Topological Sort Algorithm for Directed Acyclic Graphs, journal version listed as 2007 by the author
Ninja manual, graph tool

P5.mechanism: Recover affected vertices in prior order by sorting k vertices or scanning an interval of length L.
P5.limit: Same optimization may exist; the study requires credible edge-update traces.

E08.name: Workflow data footprint
E08.note: Alternate-path reasoning only, not the full cleanup-graph planner.

sources.title: Optimizing Workflow Data Footprint

E08.mechanism: Add cleanup tasks, group cleanup work, and remove dependencies implied by reachability.
E08.limit: Grouping can delay cleanup. Data staging limited the transfer of simulated LIGO benefits.

E10.name: Dependency-aware caching
E10.note: Least-reference-count rule only; not later coordinated cache extensions.

sources.title: Towards Dependency-Aware Cache Management for Data Analytics Applications

E10.mechanism: Extend dependency-aware caching to account for coordinated input requirements.
E10.limit: Versions, workloads, and baselines differ from the earlier LRC study.

E14.name: Parallel low-memory scheduling
E14.note: Sequential file-lifetime model; not parallel low-memory scheduling.

sources.title: Parallel Scheduling of Task Graphs with Minimal Memory Requirements

E14.mechanism: Use a sequential low-memory order to guide parallel execution.
E14.limit: Benefits depend on graph structure and the memory budget.

E15.name: Average-memory scheduling
E15.note: Peak file bytes only, not the paper’s average-memory objective or optimization.

sources.title: Minimizing Memory in Parallel Task Graph Scheduling: Focusing on Average Consumption

E15.mechanism: Optimize average consumption through exact special cases and general heuristics.
E15.limit: Average and peak memory are different objectives with different assumptions.

E17.name: Space-bounded schedulers
E17.note: Dependency layers, not cache-locality or space-bounded scheduler implementation.

sources.title: Experimental Analysis of Space-Bounded Schedulers

E17.mechanism: Use structure-aware schedules to improve locality.
E17.limit: Scheduling overhead and load balancing can erase the benefit.

E18.name: Taskiter
E18.note: No task-graph reuse or Taskiter runtime is reproduced.

sources.title: Accelerating Task-based Iterative Applications

E18.mechanism: Reuse repeated task-graph structure and bypass some scheduling work.
E18.limit: Requires repeated structure. Large task bodies can dominate scheduling overhead.

E19.name: DAG scheduling benchmark
E19.note: This is a benchmark study, not a distinct algorithm. The example is synthetic.

sources.title: Benchmarking DAG Scheduling Algorithms on Scientific Workflow Instances

E19.mechanism: Compare algorithms under common workload and machine definitions.
E19.limit: Its broad campaign is larger than this undergraduate scope.

E20.name: XLA · 2022
E20.note: Release credit and remaining-use events; compiler aliasing and special instructions are omitted.

sources.title: XLA HLO Memory List Scheduler

E20.mechanism: Rank ready instructions by released bytes minus created bytes. Update affected priorities when one user remains.
E20.limit: The greedy order is not globally optimal. Compiler aliases and live-out buffers complicate a workflow adaptation.

E23.name: Priority queue updates
E23.note: Versioned replacement entries demonstrate established heap guidance.

sources.title: Python Priority Queue Implementation Notes

E23.mechanism: Replace outdated priority entries and discard stale entries when reading the queue.
E23.limit: Stale entries still use time and memory. Tie-breaking must stay fixed.

E24.name: Montage benchmark files
E24.note: Small synthetic files, not a downloaded Montage instance or measured result.

sources.title: WfCommons Montage Execution Instances

E24.mechanism: Provide task dependencies, file relationships, and byte sizes as public JSON data.
E24.limit: File bytes are not peak RAM. These records do not contain our algorithm’s timing results.

E26.name: Tanaka and Tatebe
E26.note: Caching concept only, not the paper’s disk-cache-aware scheduling policy.

sources.title: Disk Cache-Aware Task Scheduling for Data-Intensive and Many-Task Workflow

E26.mechanism: Compare FIFO, LIFO, LIFO with Highest Rank First, and Rank with Highest Rank First.
E26.limit: Section IV-B selects the better half of repeated runs and excludes several sequential tasks. Effects depend on cache residency and processor count.

E27.name: Ceballos and colleagues
E27.note: Shows dependency timing; not a reproduction of TaskInsight measurements.

sources.title: Exploring Scheduling Effects on Task Performance with TaskInsight

E27.mechanism: Trace task scheduling decisions and examine how data reuse explains performance differences.
E27.limit: Some workloads or phases gain little; the publisher abstract alone does not support detailed effect sizes or full experimental reconstruction.

E28.name: Al-Haboobi and Kecskemeti
E28.note: Readiness only, not the function-dispatch method.

sources.title: Execution Time Reduction in Function Oriented Scientific Workflows

E28.mechanism: Alter job dispatch so dependent work can execute within the same function invocation.
E28.limit: The result includes platform and transfer effects; the full statistical methods were not audited here.

E30.name: XLA · before indexing
E30.note: Shared priority rule only, not compiler storage layout or exact code cost.

sources.title: XLA list scheduler before per-computation indexing

E30.mechanism: Cache flattened value sets, store pointer-keyed use counts and per-ready-entry vectors referencing count-map entries.
E30.limit: The later commit identifies repeated pair hashing and copied use lists, particularly for wide tuples. No performance result reproduced here.

E29.name: XLA · indexed state
E29.note: Not a reproduction of the indexed XLA change; use the code comparison for that.

sources.title: Index list scheduler buffer uses per computation, not per use

E29.mechanism: Assign dense value indices, share flattened value ranges, and let ready entries reference spans.
E29.limit: Setup, union construction and scheduling work remain. No timing comparison is supplied in the inspected commit metadata.

E31.name: Horizons
E31.note: No Horizons tracking horizons or granularity control.

sources.title: Balancing Tracking Granularity and Parallelism in Many-Task Systems: The Horizons Approach

E31.mechanism: Coalesce older tracking information using horizons while retaining a precise recent window.
E31.limit: An excessively high threshold was detrimental in a reported case; another workload changed little.

E32.name: Dominant schedules
E32.note: No dominant-schedule transformations or optimal-memory guarantee.

sources.title: New Tools for Peak Memory Scheduling

E32.mechanism: Dominant schedules support graph decomposition and parameterized algorithms.
E32.limit: Strong NP-completeness holds even for restricted graph families in this memory model.

E33.name: Joint memory scheduling

sources.title: Multiprocessor Scheduling with Memory Constraints: Fundamental Properties and Finding Optimal Solutions

E33.mechanism: Formulate the joint problem and solve instances with an integer linear program.
E33.limit: Separately optimizing parallelization and memory can be a linear factor from the joint optimum.

E34.name: LATTICE
E34.note: No NPU pipeline or memory-layout co-optimization.

sources.title: LATTICE: Constraint-Directed Scheduling, Memory Planning, and Pipeline Refinement for NPUs

E34.mechanism: A three-stage deterministic procedure combines memory-pressure scheduling, repacking and overlap.
E34.limit: The inspected evidence does not establish a general hardware result or an identical-order guarantee.

E35.name: MoSAIC
E35.note: No learned heuristic, motif recovery or LLM method is reproduced.

sources.title: MoSAIC: Learning DAG Scheduling Heuristics from Optimal Schedules through Motif-Aware Recovery and LLM-Guided Reasoning

E35.mechanism: Use optimal schedules and structural motifs to recover candidate heuristics.
E35.limit: Very recent preprint; transfer to this workload and full training cost were not independently validated here.

E36.name: Updating literature reviews
E36.note: Review-methodology paper, not an algorithm implementation. This is a basic exercise only.

sources.title: Guidelines for the Search Strategy to Update Systematic Literature Reviews in Software Engineering

E36.mechanism: Use the earlier review and primary studies as seeds for forward citation searching.
E36.limit: Their findings do not certify the coverage of this particular review.
